lessons.title: Welcome to Your Content Writing Journey
lessons.content:
Welcome to your first Content Writing lesson.

Every piece of content you read, watch, or interact with started with an idea. But turning that idea into something clear, valuable, engaging, and worth consuming is a skill.

That is where content writing comes in.

Today, you are going to build your first understanding of what content writing actually is, what a content writer does, and where content writing fits into the larger world of communication and digital content.

You will also discover that content writing is much bigger than writing blog posts.

Before we begin, make sure you have your Content Writing notes book ready.

For every lesson, take notes from the videos you watch. Don't just watch and move on. Write down important ideas, definitions, frameworks, examples, and anything you think you may need to revisit.

Your notes will become useful when you begin working on assignments, tests, and eventually your final assessments.

lessons.title: What You'll Learn Today
lessons.content:
Today, you will learn about:

1. What Content Writing Is
2. Content Writing vs Copywriting
3. What Makes Someone a Content Writer?
4. Different Types of Content Writing
5. Where Content Writers Work

lessons.title: Part 1 — What Exactly Is Content Writing?
lessons.content:
Let's start with the most important question:

What is content writing?

At its simplest, content writing is the process of creating written material designed to inform, educate, entertain, engage, or communicate with an audience.

But content writing isn't simply putting words together.

A good content writer has to understand what to say, who they're saying it to, why it matters, and how to communicate it effectively.

This is why content writing appears in so many different places—from articles and newsletters to social media content, educational materials, brand communication, and even speeches.

As you go through today's lessons, pay attention to the difference between writing words and communicating ideas.

A BRIEF OVERVIEW

Watch the lesson below, and take notes as you watch.

lessons.title: Part 1 — Content Writing for Beginners
lessons.content:
This lesson takes you through content writing from the beginning, step by step.

As you watch, take notes on the steps and write down anything you think you may need to revisit.

Don't just watch and move on.

lessons.title: Part 1 — Skills a Content Writer Must Possess
lessons.content:
This lesson covers the skills a content writer must possess.

As you watch, write down each skill.

Then think about which of them you already have, and which ones you will need to build as you go.

Take notes from the video — you will come back to these skills again as the course progresses.

lessons.title: Part 2 — Content Writing vs Other Writing Roles
lessons.content:
You will quickly discover that content writing overlaps with several other writing and content-related roles.

A copywriter may write to persuade someone to take an action.

A blogger may primarily create and publish articles around specific subjects or interests.

A scriptwriter creates written material designed to be performed or spoken, particularly for video, film, podcasts, advertisements, and other forms of media.

A social media manager, meanwhile, is responsible for much more than writing. Their role can involve content planning, publishing, community management, strategy, analytics, and overall management of a social media presence.

There can be overlap between these roles, and one person can even perform several of them.

The important thing is learning to understand what each role is primarily responsible for.

A BRIEF OVERVIEW

Watch the lesson below for the differences between content writing and copywriting.

lessons.title: Monday's Goal
lessons.content:
Today's goal is not to become an expert content writer.

It's to understand the territory you're about to enter.

By the end of today's lesson, you should be able to explain:

- What content writing is
- How content writing differs from copywriting
- How a content writer differs from other content-related roles
- What skills a content writer needs
- The different forms content writing can take
- Where content writers can work

Most importantly, start looking at the content you consume differently.

The next time you read a newsletter, scroll through a brand's social media page, watch a video script unfold, or read an article, ask yourself:

Who wrote this? Who is it for? Why was it written? And what is it trying to achieve?

That's where your journey as a content writer begins.

Take your notes. Watch the videos carefully. And welcome to Content Writing.

lessons.title: Tuesday — Understanding Audience & Purpose
lessons.content:
Welcome back to your Content Writing journey.

In our previous lesson, you were introduced to the world of content writing. You learned what content writing is, how it differs from other writing roles, the different forms it can take, and where content writers can work.

Today, we are taking the next important step.

Before you write anything, you need to know who you are writing for and why you are writing it.

A good writer doesn't simply ask, "What do I want to say?"

A good writer also asks:

"Who needs to hear this, and what should this piece of writing achieve?"

These two questions—audience and purpose—will influence almost every writing decision you make.

As always, keep your Content Writing notes book beside you. Take notes as you watch each video, especially on ideas, frameworks, examples, and questions that help you understand your audience and purpose better.

lessons.title: What You'll Learn Today — Audience & Purpose
lessons.content:
Today, you will learn how to:

1. Identify who you are writing for
2. Understand what your audience already knows
3. Identify what your audience does not know
4. Understand what your audience cares about
5. Identify the problem your content is addressing
6. Decide what you want your audience to feel
7. Decide what you want your audience to think
8. Decide what you want your audience to do

lessons.title: Part 1 — Know Your Audience
lessons.content:
Before you write, you need to know who you're talking to.

The same idea can be communicated very differently depending on who is reading it.

A beginner may need a simple explanation.

An expert may need a more advanced discussion.

A teenager may respond differently to a message than a business owner. A customer may need something different from an employee. Someone who already understands the subject will need a different approach from someone encountering it for the first time.

This is why you should never approach content with only yourself in mind.

Ask yourself:

Who am I writing for?

Then go deeper.

What does my audience already know?

What don't they know?

What do they care about?

Understanding these things helps you determine what information to include, what to explain, what language to use, and what angle will make the content relevant to them.

A BRIEF OVERVIEW

Watch the lesson below, and take notes on the questions you should ask yourself before creating content for an audience.

lessons.title: Part 1 — Finding Content Ideas for Your Audience
lessons.content:
Knowing your audience also changes where your ideas come from.

The more clearly you understand who you are writing for, the easier it becomes to find angles and topics that actually matter to them.

This lesson looks at how to find content ideas that are relevant to a specific audience rather than guessing.

A BRIEF OVERVIEW

Watch the lesson below, and take notes on how audience understanding shapes the ideas you choose to write about.

lessons.title: Part 2 — Know Your Purpose
lessons.content:
Knowing your audience is only half of the equation.

You also need to understand why the content exists in the first place.

Every piece of content should have a purpose.

Maybe you're trying to solve a problem.

Maybe you're trying to educate someone.

Maybe you want to change the way they think about something.

Maybe you want them to feel something.

Or perhaps you want them to take a specific action.

Before you begin writing, ask yourself:

What problem am I addressing?

What do I want my audience to feel?

What do I want them to think?

What do I want them to do?

These questions give your writing direction.

Without a clear purpose, you can end up with content that contains plenty of words but doesn't actually accomplish anything.

A BRIEF OVERVIEW

Watch the lesson below. Pay particular attention to how purpose influences the way content is created and communicated.

lessons.title: Putting Audience & Purpose Together
lessons.content:
Think of audience and purpose as two questions that should guide you before you write:

WHO am I writing for?

WHY am I writing this?

Your audience determines how you communicate.

Your purpose determines what you are trying to achieve.

When you understand both, your writing becomes much more intentional.

Instead of simply putting words on a page, you begin making deliberate decisions about your message, language, tone, information, structure, and call to action.

This is one of the habits that separates intentional content writers from people who simply write.

lessons.title: Tuesday's Goal
lessons.content:
By the end of today's lesson, you should understand that good writing does not begin with typing.

It begins with thinking.

Before you write your next piece of content, pause and ask:

Who am I talking to?

What do they already know?

What don't they know?

What do they care about?

Then ask:

What problem am I solving?

What do I want them to feel?

What do I want them to think?

What do I want them to do?

Make these questions part of your writing process.

The better you understand your audience and your purpose, the more effectively you can communicate with them.

Take your notes, watch both lessons carefully, and start thinking like a writer who writes for people—not just a writer who writes words.
